title: Stochastic surge resample notes
body:
Context:
Quick scratchpad for resample-based microburst experiments. Trying to reproduce noisy tails we saw in production when ingress arrivals deviate from Poisson (heavy clustering / re-sampling of past inter-arrival patterns). Goal is to find knobs (batch timeout, cold-cache fraction, dynamic vs static batching) that reduce p99 without blowing up p50 or cost.

Environment:
- Runtime image: redwood/inference-runtime:2026-02-15-rc (commit sha a1b2c3d)
- Hardware: 4xA100-40GB (dedicated small pool), 32 vCPU bench driver machine
- Model: gpt-j-6B-quant (q4_0), seq_len 1024, kv-cache enabled
- Loadgen: bench/arrival_resampler.py (local), version: v0.9.1
- Important flags used in bench runs: --qps, --burst-profile, --cold-cache-pct, --batch-timeout-ms, --batching-mode, --duration

Experiment design (high level):
1) Resample a 10-minute trace collected from Prod ingress (traceA). Create 3 resample variants: R_small (short clusters), R_med, R_heavy (high temporal clustering). Each resample repeats contiguous windows (bootstrap) to create microbursts.
2) Sweep cold-cache fraction: 0%, 20%, 50% (simulates cache priming failure due to prior evictions).
3) Sweep batch timeout: 8ms, 16ms, 32ms. Compare batching_mode: dynamic (auto batch) vs static (fixed batch 32 tokens).
4) Keep overall QPS same (125 QPS) for baseline comparability; duration = 20m each.

Command used (example):
./bench/arrival_resampler.py \
  --model gptj-6b-q4 \
  --qps 125 \
  --duration 1200 \
  --burst-profile profiles/R_med.json \
  --cold-cache-pct 20 \
  --batch-timeout-ms 16 \
  --batching-mode dynamic \
  --max-batch-tokens 4096 \
  --log-level debug

Raw perf summary (selected runs, median of 3 repetitions):
Note: p50/p95/p99 in ms, errors = % requests with non-200

Run A - R_small, cold_cache=0%, batching=dynamic, timeout=16ms:
- p50: 24 ms
- p95: 94 ms
- p99: 210 ms
- avg tokens/sec (observed): 420k tokens/s from pool
- errors: 0.07%
- notes: smooth tail, KV cache hit rate ~98% from logs

Run B - R_med, cold_cache=20%, batching=dynamic, timeout=16ms:
- p50: 26 ms
- p95: 140 ms
- p99: 740 ms
- errors: 0.8% (mostly timeouts during spike windows)
- notes: p99 spikes coincide with simultaneous cold cache misses and queues forming; observed batching jitter (one long queueing event ~850ms)

Run C - R_heavy, cold_cache=50%, batching=dynamic, timeout=16ms:
- p50: 28 ms
- p95: 320 ms
- p99: 2,100 ms
- errors: 3.5% (timeouts/retries)
- notes: catastrophic tail when cache is cold and many requests hit same prefix; dynamic batching increased batch sizes during spikes -> higher queueing latency for some requests

Run D - R_med, cold_cache=20%, batching=static(size=16), timeout=N/A:
- p50: 34 ms
- p95: 220 ms
- p99: 540 ms
- errors: 0.9%
- notes: static batching trades throughput for tighter tail; p50 higher but p99 reduced vs dynamic in same config

Run E - R_med, cold_cache=20%, batching=dynamic, timeout=8ms:
- p50: 22 ms
- p95: 170 ms
- p99: 980 ms
- notes: lower timeout reduces queue formation but increases model kernel inefficiency (less amortized tokens)

Quick percentile table (R_med, cold_cache=20%):
- timeout=8ms dynamic: p50 22ms / p95 170ms / p99 980ms
- timeout=16ms dynamic: p50 26ms / p95 140ms / p99 740ms
- static(16): p50 34ms / p95 220ms / p99 540ms

Observations / hypotheses:
- Cold cache fraction is the dominant factor for tail growth. When >20% of requests miss the KV cache, p99 skyrockets during bursts.
- Dynamic batching is great for amortizing cost and lowering p50 but can worsen p99 if bursts cause large backlogs (queueing penalty).
- Static batching or artificially capping max batch size during burst windows creates a predictable tail at the cost of some higher median latency and slightly higher unit cost.
- Lower batch timeout reduces queue build-up but increases compute inefficiency. There's a sweet spot around 12-18ms for this model/seq_len in these hardware constraints.
- Errors/timeouts are correlated with scheduler preemption and GPU warmup penalties during heavy cold-cache windows.

Notable logs/traces to inspect (ids):
- trace_run_B_2026-02-12.tgz (driver logs + runtime traces)
- flame_R_med_cold20_runB.html (flamegraph of request timeline)

Immediate actionable ideas:
- Implement a small "cold-cache fast-lane" heuristic: requests flagged as likely cold (based on prefix frequency probe) get routed to a low-latency lane with bounded batch size and higher per-request cost. Try a simple heuristic: if prefix frequency < 500 in last 10m -> fast-lane.
- Add adaptive batch cap: if queue depth > X for >Y ms, cap batch size to 32 for next T seconds (bypasses dynamic growth)
- Improve cache warming: proactive prefill for top-K prefixes before expected surge windows (trace-driven).

Next experiments (ordered):
1) Implement adaptive batch cap in bench harness (simulate cap) and rerun R_med/cold20 with timeout=12ms.
2) Fast-lane simulation: route 10% cold candidates to fast-lane, measure p99 and cost delta.
3) Sweep QPS 100->200 to validate generalization.
4) Repeat on 2xA100 vs 4xA100 to measure scaling behavior of tail under same bucketed load.

Open questions / things to sanity-check:
- Are timeouts coming from app-level (bench driver) or internal runtime scheduling? Need to correlate bench client traces with runtime request ids.
- Is KV cache eviction pattern (LRU vs CLOCK) amplifying cold windows? Check eviction logs.
- Cost impact: static/exclusive lanes will increase unit cost; quantify against SLA benefit.

Notes to self / TODO:
- Upload flamegraphs and the exact resample profiles to Gist (link above).
- Pair with Maya next week to prototype fast-lane simulation (block on her calendar).
- Add a short write-up for product about tradeoffs (1 pager): static batch vs dynamic for p99-sensitive endpoints.

End of scratchpad.

-- Kevin
